source.title: Optimal Regularization Can Mitigate Double Descent
source.authors: Preetum Nakkiran; Prayaag Venkat; S. Kakade; Tengyu Ma

page_placements.theme: More samples can hurt outside interpolation-threshold mechanisms

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test risk while varying sample or model size, and compares unregularized or underregularized models with optimally regularized ones. This tests the double-descent behavior using a regularization-focused method rather than reproducing the original studies’ full setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical monotonicity results, a numeric counterexample, and empirical risk curves. Cited findings from other work are not recorded. Values from plots are marked figure only; regularization choices used to tune the models are not separate results.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests double descent and establishes regularization conditions under which its non-monotonic shape disappears or is mitigated, qualifying the claim's scope.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: optimal L2 regularization removes double descent in specified isotropic linear models and mitigates it empirically in broader settings. Sample monotonicity under optimal scalar ridge regularization is not universal, and broader guarantees remain open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies optimal ridge or L2 regularization and compares risk across sample or model size, rather than reproducing the original studies’ full double-descent experiments. The CNN setup follows a setting from Nakkiran et al. but adds weight-decay sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes with regularization strength: unregularized or underregularized models can show non-monotonicity or double descent, whereas optimal regularization mitigates it. The optimal λ can vary with sample count or model size; in the isotropic setting it is constant across sample counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimally tuned ridge regression has expected risk below 8.157 at n=1 and above 8.179 at n=2 for the heteroscedastic two-dimensional distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional samples can worsen expected risk even with optimal scalar ridge regularization, without requiring an established interpolation-threshold mechanism.

record.problems: Empirical curve values are presented in figures without numerical point estimates in the text. The CNN result is described as largely monotonic rather than strictly monotonic, and large-weight-decay optimization instability required selecting the minimum-train-loss model among the last 5K steps. The non-isotropic ridge monotonicity claim without a modified regularizer remains a conjecture.

untested.parts: No test-error trajectory over training epochs is reported.
The heteroscedastic counterexample does not establish that its risk increase occurs near an interpolation threshold.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak locations across axes.
No systematic noise or variance intervention establishes the causal origin of peaks. Strict peak elimination in CNNs and universal elimination across distributions are not established.
No reparameterization by effective parameter count tests whether double descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Theorem 2 proves sample monotonicity for every fixed ridge parameter at least as large as the optimum in the isotropic Gaussian setting; mitigation does not require exact optimal tuning.

The authors state sample monotonicity for non-isotropic Gaussian regression with a covariance-dependent regularizer. Record the claimed result with the source's formula inconsistency: Equation 20 and Theorem 5 specify Σ⁻¹, whereas Lemma 5's change of variables with M=I yields a Σ penalty.
missing.locator: Section 6.1; Appendix A.3, Lemma 5 and Theorem 5

record.verdict_notes: This study is not either listed original source. States for regularized rows describe the presence of double descent or sample-wise worsening; their absence can support V6. Figure shapes are assessed from the authors' explicit descriptions because the supplied text contains captions but no readable plotted values.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests model-size behavior in random ReLU features and CNNs, but not a broad sweep of deep-network architectures or training epochs.

The paper tests sample-wise behavior in selected ridge and random-feature settings, but does not establish that any increase in error occurs specifically near an interpolation threshold in every setting.
Tests include linear regression, random ReLU features, and CNNs, but do not cover all model classes or establish a universal capacity-risk curve.

The study tests whether optimal regularization mitigates double descent and reports one triple-descent setting. It does not systematically test whether label noise or variance drives peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes peaks across settings.

rows.value: R(β̂n+1opt) ≤ R(β̂nopt), for all β* ∈ R^d, d ∈ N, n ∈ N, σ > 0

rows.subject: ridge regression on random projected features
rows.size_stated: model size d ≤ p; all p ∈ N
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 3 compares expected test risk for model sizes d and d+1, with ridge regularization tuned optimally for each size.

conditions.value: random d-dimensional orthonormal projection followed by linear regression

rows.value: R(β̂d+1opt) ≤ R(β̂dopt), for all p ∈ N, θ ∈ R^p, d ≤ p, n ∈ N, σ > 0

rows.subject: optimally-regularized ridge regression on a two-dimensional counterexample distribution
rows.operation_detail: Compares expected test risk using n = 1 versus n = 2 samples, with the ridge parameter optimized for each n.

conditions.value: (e1, 1) with probability 1 − ε; (e2, ±A) with probability ε

rows.baseline: For n = 1, R(β̂n=1opt) < 8.157, achieved with λ = 400/2401 ≈ 0.166597
rows.value: For n = 2, R(β̂n=2opt) > 8.179, achieved with λ = 0.642525
rows.note: The n = 2 optimal risk is numerically confirmed via Mathematica; the paper does not state that this example is specifically at an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: The recorded increase is real, so 'reversed' is incorrect. However, the text does not establish proximity to an interpolation threshold or a double-descent peak; it therefore does not directly test V3 or peak elimination under V6.

statements.correction: Theorems 1 and 3 establish sample-wise and model-wise monotonicity under their respective isotropic Gaussian assumptions. Sections 5.1–5.2 report monotonicity or prevention of double descent for Fashion-MNIST random ReLU features. Figure 2 reports means over 5000 trials. Publication-review status is unstated in the supplied study text.
statements.problem: The study-specific monotonicity results and controls are supported; this study's reviewed status cannot be verified from the supplied text.

statements.correction: Theorems 1 and 3 establish the stated conditional monotonicity results. Section 5.1 reports unregularized peaks near n=15 and n=d=30 and empirical monotonicity with optimal tuning. Section 5.2 reports substantial CNN mitigation without establishing strict elimination. Preetum Nakkiran also authors the cited original deep-double-descent study. Publication-review status is unstated in the supplied study text.
